introduction-the-cloud-has-a-physical-fo.core: The cloud is millions of physical servers consuming electricity and water and producing heat. Software decisions directly drive energy use and emissions.

first_principles.problem: Engineers treat compute as weightless, ignoring that data centres use around 1–2% of global electricity.
derivation: Run **where and when** electricity is clean.

analogy.title: A city of refrigerators
analogy.story: Each server is a fridge that never turns off, and someone has to power and cool them all.
analogy.breaks: Cloud providers' efficiency gains help, but demand growth outpaces them.

example.title: An idle dev cluster
flow: Schedule shutdown → cost and carbon cut

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: FinOps and GreenOps often point the same way.

example.outcome: software is seen as having physical impact.

check.q: Why do FinOps and GreenOps often align?
check.a: Eliminating waste reduces both the money spent and the energy consumed.

the-core-problem-carbon-intensity-of-ele.core: Carbon intensity (gCO₂e per kWh) varies hugely by grid region and by hour, with hydro or wind-heavy grids far cleaner than coal-heavy ones. The same workload's emissions depend on where and when it runs.

first_principles.problem: Identical workloads emit 10–50x more CO₂ in some regions than others, and nobody considers this.
truths: Renewable output varies with weather and time.

analogy.title: Two identical kettles on different power
analogy.story: One powered by a hydro dam, the other by a coal plant: same tea, very different smoke.
analogy.breaks: Latency, data residency and cost also constrain where you can run.

example.title: Choosing a region for batch ML
flow: Same job, ~95% less CO₂ in B

steps.label: Decision
steps.detail: Run training in B, where latency doesn't matter.

check.a: Grams of CO₂-equivalent emitted per kilowatt-hour of electricity on a grid.

carbon-aware-computing-shifting-the-load.core: Carbon-aware software shifts flexible work in time (run when the grid is cleanest) or space (run in the cleanest region), and can shape demand (lower quality or batch more when the grid is dirty).

first_principles.problem: Batch jobs run at fixed times regardless of whether the grid is coal- or wind-powered at that moment.
derivation: **Time shifting**: schedule batch work in the clean windows forecast ahead.
**Location shifting**: route flexible jobs to cleaner regions.
**Demand shaping**: degrade gracefully when the grid is dirty.
Use the **Carbon Aware SDK / KEDA scalers**.

analogy.title: Running the dishwasher at night on cheap, clean power
analogy.story: The dishes get cleaned either way; timing changes the cost and the emissions.
analogy.breaks: Latency-sensitive, user-facing work usually can't shift.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Same work, same deadline, less carbon.

check.q: What kinds of workloads suit carbon-aware time shifting?
check.a: Deferrable ones like batch processing, ML training, backups and CI for non-urgent work.

power-efficiency-optimization-the-hardwa.core: Doing the same work with less energy is the other lever: ARM processors like Graviton use up to ~60% less energy for the same performance, along with right-sizing, high utilisation, efficient languages and accelerators.

first_principles.problem: Fleets run on power-hungry x86 instances at 10% utilisation.
truths: Energy per operation differs by architecture.
Idle servers still draw substantial power.
derivation: **Optimise hot code paths** and pick efficient runtimes.

analogy.title: Swapping incandescent bulbs for LEDs
analogy.story: Same light, a fraction of the electricity.
analogy.breaks: Migration needs multi-arch builds and testing, and some software isn't ARM-ready.

check.q: Why does high utilisation improve energy efficiency?
check.a: Idle servers still draw significant power, so consolidating work means fewer machines for the same output.

measuring-success-pue-vs-sci.core: PUE measures data-centre facility efficiency (total facility energy / IT energy), which is the provider's concern. SCI (Software Carbon Intensity, from the Green Software Foundation) measures carbon per functional unit of your software: ((E × I) + M) per R.

first_principles.problem: 'Be greener' without a metric is a slogan, and PUE doesn't reflect your software's choices.
truths: Facility overhead and software efficiency are separate.
derivation: **SCI** = ((Energy × Intensity) + Embodied) per functional unit R.

analogy.title: Building insulation vs. appliance efficiency
analogy.story: PUE is how well the building is insulated; SCI is how efficiently your own appliances do their job.
analogy.breaks: Energy measurement in the cloud is often estimated, so be consistent.

steps.label: Use
steps.detail: A release that halves energy halves the operational part of SCI.

check.q: What does the M term in SCI represent?
check.a: Embodied emissions: the carbon from manufacturing the hardware, allocated to the software's use of it.
